projects.name: Field Operations Platform
projects.description: Production field-operations platform for a landscaping company: crew dispatch, timeclock and GPS tracking, fleet, inventory and payroll, with a React dashboard and a WhatsApp AI agent, running on Oracle Cloud and PostgreSQL.
projects.overview: A landscaping and construction crew was coordinating schedules, equipment loadouts, material orders and check-ins through scattered group chats, spreadsheets and memory. I built a single system that holds that data, and two ways to use it from a phone: a web dashboard for managers and a WhatsApp assistant for crews. I wrote the backend, adapted the frontend, deploy it, and keep it running.
highlights: 40+ database migrations, a TypeScript domain layer and a REST API behind a React dashboard
WhatsApp crew assistant that calls the same domain logic through an MCP server
Nightly backups with restores actually tested, health heartbeats and a disaster-recovery runbook

sections.title: Architecture
bullets: Backend: a TypeScript/Node.js domain layer (crew, sites, equipment, inventory, timeclock, procurement, payroll) exposed two ways: a REST facade for the dashboard and an MCP server for AI agents. Both call the same domain functions, so business rules live in one place.
Data: PostgreSQL (with pgvector) in a container, schema managed by ordered migrations, with a nightly dump copied to cloud object storage.
Frontend: an open-source construction-ERP frontend, forked and pruned down to the eight modules the business uses, served as static files by Caddy.
Edge: Cloudflare in front, full-strict TLS with an origin certificate, Caddy as the reverse proxy on a small Oracle Cloud VM.
Crew interface: a WhatsApp gateway connected to the MCP server, so crews can check in, log photos, order materials and ask questions in plain language.

sections.title: The WhatsApp agent and how it is kept safe
bullets: Every action is a typed tool that declares a capability tier: 0 for read-only lookups, 2 for crew submissions (time clock, receipts, mileage, check-outs), 3 for anything that commits money, schedule or inventory, and 4 for admin and financial actions.

The gateway holds one service credential limited to tier 2, attached by the gateway so the language model never sees it. I tested a tier-3 call with that credential against the real server and it was denied.
Credentials are signed capability grants tied to an identity, and revoking a grant is the safety valve if one is ever exposed.
Some crew actions, such as spend records and mileage claims, use confirm-before-execute: the submission becomes a pending confirmation that a manager approves or rejects before anything is committed.
The agent resolves who is writing by looking up the sender's phone number with a tool, and it only reports what a tool returns, not what it guesses.
A policy file states which functions may call external services, and the AI provider chain has fallbacks if one provider fails.

sections.title: Security and reliability
bullets: Login rate limiting plus per-account lockout, and TOTP multi-factor authentication for admin accounts.
Dependency audit clean, and the git history scanned for committed secrets (none found).
Heartbeat health checks from the server and an independent external uptime monitor.
Nightly database backups, and a restore into a throwaway database to prove the backup holds real, coherent data.

sections.title: A real outage, and what changed
paragraphs: A frontend build run on the 1 GB production VM exhausted memory and made the server unresponsive for over an hour. I recovered it under time pressure, then wrote a disaster-recovery runbook. Builds now happen on my own machine and are shipped as static files, and the backup restore test that was previously just a gap in the plan is now done for real.

projects.name: Business IT Stack
projects.description: Self-hosted business IT stack: single sign-on, helpdesk, ERP, file sharing, mail and a password vault behind Cloudflare Access, with AI-agent admin tools built as MCP servers.
projects.overview: A small company ran almost everything through WhatsApp and personal accounts. I designed and built a self-hosted stack of open-source services behind one login, and a set of MCP tools so day-to-day administration can happen from the same WhatsApp chat the staff already use. It is running in my homelab and was written up as a proposal for the business.
highlights: Authentik single sign-on (OIDC) in front of Nextcloud, Zammad, Odoo and Vault
Nothing is exposed directly: Cloudflare Access, an outbound-only tunnel and one reverse proxy
MCP admin servers built from scratch and tested against the real products

sections.title: What is in the stack
bullets: Authentik: identity provider with MFA and OIDC for every other app.
Nextcloud: files and sharing. Zammad: helpdesk and ticketing. Odoo Community: ERP, CRM and timesheets. Vault: secrets and signing keys.
Mail: Stalwart mail server with Roundcube webmail on a separate cloud VM, with inbound mail delivered through Cloudflare Email Routing and an outbound relay.
Traefik routes by hostname on a private Docker network; each app has its own database and only Traefik publishes a port.

sections.title: How a request is protected
paragraphs: A request passes the Cloudflare edge, then Cloudflare Access (one-time e-mail PIN with an allow-list), then an outbound-only tunnel into the VM, then Traefik, then the app, which sends the user to Authentik for single sign-on with a password and TOTP. The tunnel is outbound-only, so nothing on the VM is published to the internet.

Only Authentik's protocol endpoints (token, userinfo and key discovery) bypass the Access wall, because the apps' servers must call them directly. Those calls still require a client secret or bearer token.

sections.title: Mail without opening port 25
paragraphs: The cloud provider blocks inbound port 25 at its edge, so inbound mail is received by Cloudflare Email Routing, handed to a Worker, posted over HTTPS to a small bridge on the mail VM and passed to Stalwart with the original sender's address preserved. Outbound mail goes through an authenticated relay with SPF and DKIM.

sections.title: Administering it from WhatsApp
bullets: The goal was to let staff rarely open the service UIs: an `it-admin` MCP server plus thin servers for Zammad, Authentik, Stalwart and Odoo, all driven by the company's WhatsApp assistant.
Safety by construction: the tools have no operation for passwords, recovery links, tokens or keys, and refuse to touch superusers and service accounts.
Tiered actions with staged approval: risky changes wait for an out-of-chat approval, which re-authenticates the approver through Authentik with MFA and is valid only for that one action.

Testing: each MCP server has unit tests, mutation checks, and live tests run against real instances of the product, not only mocks. Testing against real response shapes caught a bug that convenient mocks had hidden.

sections.title: Status and what I would do next
paragraphs: The stack is built and running on a lab host; at the last update, finishing the single sign-on wiring and final hardening were still open. Deploying it for the business is a proposal, not a finished rollout. Next steps are finishing the SSO wiring, a restore drill for the whole stack, and moving it to always-on hosting.

projects.name: Homelab
projects.description: Two-site homelab: a Raspberry Pi 5 running always-on services and a Windows Server host running Hyper-V, joined by a Tailscale mesh with monitoring, encrypted backups and written runbooks.
projects.overview: I built a homelab to practise what a small IT team does: networking, monitoring, backups, identity, and documentation. A Raspberry Pi 5 runs the services that must always be up, a Windows Server 2022 machine runs the heavier workloads, and the two reach each other and my cloud servers over Tailscale. Everything is documented as runbooks, and the monitoring is defined in git.
highlights: 28 service monitors defined in git, with phone alerts and an external backstop check
Tailscale mesh: SSH and admin services are reachable only on the private network
Encrypted, pull-based backups of every machine, with a documented restore plan

sections.title: Layout
bullets: Raspberry Pi 5 (wired): DNS and ad blocking with AdGuard Home, Uptime Kuma, ntfy push alerts, a Tailscale node, and a small website behind a Cloudflare Tunnel.
Windows Server 2022 host: Hyper-V runs the IT-stack VM on a schedule; the host also runs a media server and has GNS3 installed for CCNA practice.
Two Oracle Cloud VMs host the field-operations platform and the mail server; both are reachable over SSH only through Tailscale.
A Wi-Fi repeater in router mode gives the server its own subnet and internet access, because the server has no Wi-Fi of its own.

sections.title: Networking and access
paragraphs: Devices sit on the home network, the repeater's private subnet and a Tailscale overlay. Services such as the password manager, SSH and RDP are tailnet-only, with firewall rules scoped to the lab subnet and Tailscale's address range. From anywhere, I connect through Tailscale instead of opening ports.

sections.title: Monitoring
paragraphs: Uptime Kuma on the Pi checks 28 targets: the machines, the website, the field-operations platform, mail, SSH on the cloud servers and each IT-stack service. Alerts go to my phone through ntfy, and backups report in with a success or failure heartbeat. A timer on a cloud VM checks the public site from outside, because if the Pi goes down so does its monitoring.
Known gaps are written down: the monitoring depends on the Pi, and the password manager does not yet have its own monitor.

sections.title: Backups
paragraphs: Backups are pulled, not pushed: the server fetches each machine's data over SSH using keys restricted to that job, checks the streams, encrypts them with an authenticated scheme and copies the result off-site to cloud storage, weekly and on demand. The first full backup set completed and verified. A full restore drill has not been done yet, and the documentation says so.

sections.title: Design changes and lessons
paragraphs: The first design had the Pi route a separate lab subnet over a cable. It was dropped because the USB Ethernet adapter it needed was never bought and the Pi's Wi-Fi roaming kept causing outages, so the Pi moved to a wired connection and the server went behind the repeater. The changelog records both designs and why one replaced the other.

Alongside the build I wrote operations docs, a troubleshooting log of real incidents, a service-by-service reference with diagrams, and an offline study set (phone e-books and 588 flashcards) so the whole environment can be learned and rebuilt.
